idiom_name: Validating named constructor: private/passkey ctor + static create() returning std::expected
implementation_notes: C++'s own construction machinery enforces the Essence invariant directly, so the classic two-class protocol usually collapses into one class: make every constructor private (or passkey-guarded), declare the Essence/factory a friend or a static member, and expose a named constructor create() that validates all compulsory properties BEFORE instantiating the target - returning std::expected<Contract, Error> (C++23, value()/std::unexpected name the failing property) or std::optional<Contract> (C++17) instead of throwing from the constructor. C++17 guaranteed copy elision makes the validate-then-construct return-by-value shape free, and constexpr validation can even reject literal inputs at compile time. The full classic form is still justified when property collection is genuinely multi-step or interactive (form-style clients needing validateParameters() feedback): there the Essence becomes a small parameter bundle (struct or builder) that carries and checks the values until create() consumes it.
pitfalls: std::make_shared/std::make_unique and optional/expected in_place or emplace paths cannot call a PRIVATE constructor even when your factory is a friend - the allocation helper inside the wrapper is not a friend. Use the passkey idiom instead: a public constructor taking a marker type whose default constructor is private, so only the class (and make_shared) can invoke it while outside callers cannot.

The passkey/marker tag must not be an aggregate: before C++20, an empty tag with only defaulted constructors allows aggregate initialization such as Contract({}, c, s), silently bypassing the restriction - give the tag a private default constructor to block it.

Mixed creation conventions reintroduce the problem the pattern avoids: some factories throwing std::invalid_argument while others return std::unexpected forces clients into exception-driven control flow for ordinary validation feedback. Pick std::expected/std::optional for expected invalid input and reserve exceptions for truly exceptional failures.

Returning the target by value requires it to be movable or elidable: a direct prvalue return is free since C++17, but any local-then-return path needs a move constructor - a type with deleted moves breaks the factory. std::expected<T, E> itself additionally requires T to be movable or copyable.

friend grants the Essence the target's ENTIRE private surface, tempting validation logic to live only in the friend and drift from the target's own invariants (the dual-validation trap). Prefer narrow authorization - a passkey parameter authorizes exactly one constructor instead of exposing all members.
